title: Phase 2: task dependency system + Gantt rendering
body:
From the ecosystem ROADMAP (§1, ref #3695).

## What
Add a **task dependency system** to task-cli and **Gantt** rendering on top of it.

- Tasks can declare dependencies on other tasks (blocks / blocked-by edges).
- Render a Gantt-style view of the dependency graph (timeline + blocking relationships).
- Surface external-to-session deps (tasks the session depends on but did not create).

## Why
Phase 1 gives flat per-session task tracking. Real agent work has ordering constraints; without a dependency graph the agent cannot reason about what unblocks what, and the user has no at-a-glance view of the critical path.

## Acceptance
- A task can be created/updated with `blocked-by`/`blocks` edges; cycles rejected.
- `task list`/a dedicated view renders the graph as a Gantt (ASCII or image).
- The Gantt-render primitive is reusable (it will later move to the shared lib — see agent-tools shared-lib tracking issue).

Depends on Phase 1 foundation landing.

title: Daemon service + webhooks (adapter-based trackers)
body:
From the ecosystem ROADMAP (§1 Phase 2, ref #3695).

## What
A long-lived **daemon service** for task-cli (modeled on tg-ctl): the first CLI call brings it up; it survives restarts/kills; it subscribes to backend **webhooks**.

- **adapter-based**: GitHub Issues and Linear today, pluggable for future trackers.
- Subscribes to gh-issues / Linear webhooks to keep task state live without polling.
- Daemon-supervisor logic (survive kills) is shared with tg-ctl — it will move to the agent-tools shared lib (`daemon-supervisor`); build it here first, extract later.

## Why
Phase-1 task state is pull-only. Live webhook subscription lets the agent react to external task changes (a dependency closed elsewhere, a due date set in Linear) without the agent re-polling, and is the substrate for completion/due notifications (separate issue).

## Acceptance
- First `task` invocation auto-starts the daemon; it survives a kill and re-spawns on next call.
- Webhook subscription wired for at least the GitHub Issues adapter; Linear adapter behind the same interface.
- Adapter interface documented so a new tracker is a drop-in.

title: Completion + due-date notifications via tmux-inject
body:
From the ecosystem ROADMAP (§1 Phase 2, ref #3695).

## What
When a task completes, inject a "done, X unblocked" line into the agent's tmux pane (via the shared-lib `tmux-inject`, extracted from tg-ctl). Plus **due-date reminders** delivered to the agent the same way.

## Why
The agent should learn that finishing task A unblocked B/C without re-querying, and should be nudged about due dates. Pushing this into the agent's tmux pane is how tg-ctl already surfaces inbound events.

## Acceptance
- On a task transitioning to done, dependents are recomputed and a "done, <deps> unblocked" message is injected into the originating agent's tmux pane.
- Due-date reminders fire to the agent ahead of the due time.
- Injection respects the pending-question DEFER rule (see tg-cli decisions-as-buttons issue) — never blast text into an open interactive prompt.
- Built on the daemon (separate issue) and the shared `tmux-inject` primitive.

title: Integrations: tg classify hook, agent-tools ticket-discipline skill, rig provisioning
body:
From the ecosystem ROADMAP (§1 Integrations).

## What
Wire task-cli into the rest of the ecosystem:

- **tg-cli classify inbound hook** (ref #3645): an inbound TG message classified as actionable feeds task-cli. Needs a NEW `on-inbound` hook point in `agents-hooks/v1`.
- **agent-tools `strict-ticket-discipline` skill** + a `require-ticket-before-commit` guard (optionally a `ci/ticket-required` check). (Tracked too in the agent-tools harvest issue.)
- **rig provisioning**: rig installs linear-cli when `backend=linear` (auth only).
- **task-cli self-hook** so the tool advertises/installs its own hook.

## Why
task-cli is only useful if tickets are created at the right moments (inbound triage, pre-commit discipline) and if the backend auth is provisioned automatically.

## Acceptance
- New `on-inbound` hook point exists in `agents-hooks/v1` and tg-cli can route a classified inbound message to task-cli.
- `strict-ticket-discipline` skill + `require-ticket-before-commit` guard exist (coordinate with agent-tools harvest issue).
- `rig apply` installs linear-cli when the configured backend is Linear.

title: Add task new / task done verb aliases (CTO-requested ergonomics) + fix ruff
body:
## What
task ships create + status <id> done as the create/close verbs, but the CTO asks for 'task new' and 'task done' specifically. Add 'new' as an alias of create and 'done' as a close-by-id command, and clean the 5 pre-existing ruff F401/F841 errors so the ship-gate is green.

## Why (motivation)
The CTO explicitly asked for 'task new' / 'task done' ('когда ты уже доделаешь и внедришь везде таск cli'). The current create/status-done verbs work but don't match the requested muscle-memory; a tool he won't reach for isn't adopted. Ruff is also not clean on main (5 errors) which blocks the review/ship gate.

## User impact
Alex (CTO) and every agent get the exact verbs they reach for first ('task new ...', 'task done 123'); the ship-gate passes ruff so the change can land.

## Cost of inaction
The CTO keeps hitting 'unknown command new/done' and falls back to raw gh issue, defeating the whole enforced-ticket point; ruff stays red and every future PR's gate fails on unrelated lint.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] task new --title ... creates a ticket identically to task create (proved by a unit test asserting cmd_new dispatches cmd_create)
- [ ] task done <id> closes the ticket via the DONE transition running the on-done gates (proved by a unit test against the FakeBackend)
- [ ] ruff check . exits 0 (proved by CI smoke + local run)
- [ ] task --help lists new and done; install-skill SKILL.md mentions them

title: done/change/status close paths don't validate the source-state transition
body:
## What
task done / change --done / status <id> done all set State.DONE and run the on-done GATES, but none validate that the CURRENT state legally permits the transition (tasklib/cli.py cmd_done ~line 1010, cmd_change ~890, cmd_status ~960). So 'task done' on an already-done or cancelled ticket silently re-closes it: re-runs update() + _attach_screenshots(), and could 'resurrect' a cancelled ticket to done. Surfaced by the review-gate (claude-opus-4-8) on PR for issue #8.

## Why (motivation)
An idempotent-looking close that actually re-writes a cancelled ticket to done is a correctness footgun: it can flip a deliberately-cancelled ticket back to done and re-fire side effects (attachments, logs). The three close verbs share this gap, so the behavior is at least consistent — but consistent-wrong.

## User impact
An agent or the CTO closing an id without checking its current state can silently un-cancel work or double-close; the ticket history then misrepresents what happened.

## Cost of inaction
Cancelled tickets can be silently revived to done; double-close re-fires attachments/log events; the audit trail lies about the lifecycle.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] task done / change --done / status done on an already-DONE ticket is a no-op-with-notice (or a clean error), not a silent re-write (proved by a unit test per verb)
- [ ] the same on a CANCELLED ticket refuses with a clear message unless explicitly forced (proved by a unit test)
- [ ] the legal-transition check lives in ONE shared helper, not duplicated across the three close paths (DRY)

## Screenshots
(none)

title: install-skill must also write the .blurbs/<tool>.md SessionStart blurb
body:
## What
tasklib/install.py:install_skill() writes ~/.agents/skills/task/SKILL.md but never writes ~/.agents/skills/.blurbs/task.md. The siblings draw/tg/review each ship a .blurbs/<tool>.md; a SessionStart hook in ~/.claude/settings.json cats every .blurbs/*.md into each new session ('Agent CLI tools installed on this machine'). Without the blurb, task is installed but NOT advertised at session start the way its siblings are.

## Why (motivation)
task-cli was rolled out 'everywhere' to mirror its siblings; the missing blurb means every new agent session does NOT auto-see task while it DOES see draw/tg/review. The rollout is incomplete and silently so.

## User impact
Agents/sessions on this and any other machine running 'task install-skill' do not get task surfaced at SessionStart, so they fall back to raw 'gh issue' instead of the enforced ticket interface.

## Cost of inaction
task stays a second-class citizen vs its siblings — installed but invisible at session start; the 'internon everywhere' goal is not actually met and regresses on every fresh machine.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] install_skill() also writes ~/.agents/skills/.blurbs/task.md (created if the dir is missing)
- [ ] the blurb is a one-line '- `task` — ...' entry matching the sibling format
- [ ] install-skill is idempotent: re-running it does not rewrite an already-current blurb
- [ ] a unit test asserts the blurb file is written with the task marker

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- Session: session:2

title: install-skill is a 1-layer stub: missing blurb + harness-instruction injection that all sibling CLIs do
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
task-cli shipped v1 with install-skill writing ONLY ~/.agents/skills/task/SKILL.md. The sibling personal CLIs (draw/review/tg) use a 3-layer install_agent_skill(name, skill_md, blurb): (1) SKILL.md + .blurbs/<tool>.md, (2) a marked <!-- skill:<tool> --> block appended to each detected harness instruction file (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md etc.), (3) an idempotent SessionStart aggregator hook. task-cli does only layer 1, so task is NOT advertised the same way as its siblings: no .blurbs/task.md (the always-on, every-session blurb the SessionStart aggregator cats), no CLAUDE.md block, no ~/.claude/skills symlink.

## User impact
Agents do not get task surfaced in every session the way draw/review/tg are. The whole point of task-cli (every request becomes a ticket) depends on agents being aware of it at session start; with only SKILL.md, discovery is weaker and inconsistent with the sibling rollout the CTO expects.

## Cost of inaction
Future machine bootstraps (curl install.sh on a new box) will under-advertise task: the tool installs on PATH but never injects the always-on blurb, so agents keep using raw gh issue / linear instead. The inconsistency compounds every new environment.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] tasklib/install.py install_skill writes all 3 layers matching the siblings: (a) ~/.agents/skills/task/SKILL.md AND ~/.agents/skills/.blurbs/task.md, (b) a marked block in each detected harness instruction file, (c) idempotent SessionStart aggregator hook (skip if already present, never clobber unparseable settings.json), plus the ~/.claude/skills/task compat symlink. Idempotent (safe re-run). A test asserts the blurb file + SKILL.md are written into a tmp HOME. ruff + pytest + mypy green.

(none)

title: Docker integration test: real cheap LLM agent verifies task-cli is advertised + usable (CI test-cli job)
body:
## What

A hermetic, Docker-based integration test proving end-to-end that `task` works on a fresh machine: a container provisions the CLI via the real install path, a special test repo holds a trivial feature request, and a **deterministic non-LLM smoke** plus a **gated real-cheap-LLM-agent** test verify task-cli is **advertised** (a fresh agent discovers `task` as a skill / in the SessionStart blurb) and **usable** (`task new`/`task list` work against the backend).

## Why / motivation

We claim "a fresh agent discovers and uses `task`" but nothing proves it end-to-end on a clean machine. install-skill could regress (blurb dropped — cf #13/#14), the SessionStart surfacing could break, or a real agent could keep reaching for raw `gh issue`. Only a real-agent-in-a-clean-container test catches these.

## User impact if not done

Silent regressions in discoverability/usability ship undetected: agents stop being told `task` exists, or `task` breaks against the backend, and we find out from a confused agent in production, not CI.

## Scope (CTO, tg#4580): NO commit-gate

Do **NOT** test/assert a require-ticket commit-blocking gate. Only **advertised** + **usable**. The CTO does not want a commit-blocking ticket gate here.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `test/docker/` harness: Dockerfile + entrypoint that installs `task` via its real `install.sh` (runs `task install-skill`) and wires the same SessionStart blurb hook a real machine uses.
- A special test git repo (in-container) with a trivial feature request.
- **Deterministic smoke (no LLM, runs in normal CI):** asserts (a) `~/.agents/skills/.blurbs/task.md` + `~/.agents/skills/task/SKILL.md` are written by the real install (advertised), (b) the SessionStart hook surfaces the `task` blurb, (c) `task new`/`task list` succeed against a hermetic backend.
- **Full real-agent test (gated behind an API-key secret, runs on PR merge):** a cheap model (claude-haiku via `claude -p`) asked to track a request DISCOVERS `task` (it appears in available skills / the SessionStart blurb) and USES `task` rather than raw `gh issue`. Skips with a clear message when the secret is absent.
- A CI job `test-cli` wired to run on PR merge (trigger documented). Deterministic smoke unconditional; real-agent step gated on the secret.
- The deterministic smoke is verified to pass locally (docker build + non-LLM assertions).

## Cost of inaction

Discoverability/usability of the team's enforced ticket interface rots unnoticed.

## Out of scope

Commit-blocking ticket gate (explicitly excluded by CTO). The rig ecosystem-provisioning branch is referenced but not a runtime dependency.

title: Harden the Docker real-agent leg: force cheap model onto the `task` CLI (defeat TaskCreate/TodoWrite collision)
body:
## What

Follow-up to #15. The Docker integration harness ships a real-cheap-agent leg (`test/docker/agent_test.sh`) that drives `claude -p` (haiku) and asserts the agent discovers + USES the `task` CLI to file a ticket. The deterministic leg is a proven gate; the **real-agent leg is not yet** — it runs gated + `continue-on-error` in CI.

## The gap (observed against a live haiku)

- The agent correctly does NOT use raw `gh issue create` (assertion (a) passes).
- But haiku resolves the **harness's own built-in to-do/task tool** (`TodoWrite` / `TaskCreate`) over the advertised `task` CLI, so no ticket lands in the backend → the 'a ticket was created via task' assertion (b) fails (`before=0 after=0`).
- Root cause: a name collision between 'task' the concept and the `task` CLI, plus a cheap model's bias toward a built-in tool over a shell command. `--disallowedTools` with bare names did not reliably block the built-in.

## Why / user impact if not done

Without this, we only *deterministically* prove `task` is advertised + usable; we do NOT yet prove a real fresh agent actually CHOOSES `task` over its built-ins. That last mile is the whole point of an agent-in-the-loop test — otherwise discoverability can regress (agent silently prefers a built-in) and CI stays green.

## Cost of inaction

The real-agent assertion stays non-fatal/unproven; a regression where agents stop choosing `task` ships undetected.

## Acceptance criteria

- The real-agent leg, run with a real `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` against the in-container mock, RELIABLY makes the agent file the ticket via the `task` CLI (a ticket lands in the mock backend, task-shaped), across a few runs.
- Built-in to-do/task tools are provably disabled for the run (verify the exact tool name(s) and the working `--disallowedTools`/`--tools` syntax), OR the prompt is made collision-proof so the model picks the shell `task` path unprompted-by-name.
- Once reliable, flip `continue-on-error: true` OFF on the `real-agent` CI job so it becomes a real gate on the credentialed merge run.
- Validated with a recorded run (transcript + the mock backend showing the created ticket).

## Notes

- The harness, mock GitHub server, deterministic assertions, and CI scaffold already exist (#15). This is purely hardening the LLM leg's prompt/tool-gating + a live-key validation.

comments.body:
Hardening landed in PR (feat/harden-agent-leg-and-enforce-assert): the TodoWrite/TaskCreate/Task collision is now structurally gated and the **key-free part is asserted in the DETERMINISTIC leg** (runs on every PR, no key, not hidden behind the credentialed + continue-on-error agent leg).

What's done (shippable, validated without a live key):
- Tool gating split into `test/docker/agent_tools_gating.sh` (single source of truth): `--disallowedTools TodoWrite TaskCreate Task` (canonical, space-separated per `claude --help`) + `--allowedTools Bash Read`; plus `--tools "Bash,Read"` (comma form) added ONLY when `claude --help` advertises `--tools` (anchored grep).
- Collision-proof prompt: names the affordance concretely (run the `task` SHELL command via Bash) and forbids any built-in todo/task/scratchpad tool; still does NOT spell out the subcommand.
- The gating CONFIG self-check (`agent_tools_gating.sh --check`) now runs in the deterministic leg via entrypoint step 2c — a regression that drops a built-in from the denylist (or leaks one into the allowlist) fails a normal PR, key-free. Validated in-container.

Still open (the LIVE-key validation — NOT provable without a key, so the leg stays gated + `continue-on-error: true`):
- Confirm real `claude` parses `--allowedTools`/`--disallowedTools` as a SPACE-separated variadic (so `--disallowedTools TodoWrite TaskCreate Task` denies all three, not just the first). The deterministic check proves the argv we BUILD, not how the CLI PARSES it.
- Confirm `--tools` (comma) passed ALONGSIDE `--allowedTools`/`--disallowedTools` (space) composes cleanly on the target build rather than one restriction model overriding the other.
- A recorded run proving haiku reliably lands a backend ticket via `task` across a few runs (transcript + mock backend showing the ticket).

Flip `continue-on-error: false` on the `real-agent` job once the above live-key run is recorded.

title: Docker test-cli: assert require-ticket enforcement end-to-end in the deterministic leg
body:
## What

Now that `require-ticket-before-commit` is **strict + live** (agent-tools#95, rig-provisioned), the Docker `test-cli` harness (`test/docker/`) should ALSO assert the enforcement end-to-end in the clean-rig container — not just that `task` is advertised + usable.

Add to the **DETERMINISTIC leg** (no LLM needed — it's a git-commit + hook assertion, so it runs on every PR):

- A commit WITHOUT a ticket reference is **BLOCKED**: the hook exits **10** and emits the stable `[require-ticket] BLOCKED: no ticket reference` marker.
- A commit WITH a ticket reference (`Closes #1`, or a `task`-created ticket id) **PASSES**: the hook exits 0 / `decision: allow`.

This is the commit-blocking enforcement piece that #15's harness deferred (it was advertise-only, scoped to advertised+usable per CTO tg#4580). Now that the gate is strict + rig-provisioned, prove it.

## Why / user impact if not done

The harness proves `task` is advertised + usable, but does NOT prove the require-ticket *enforcement* actually blocks a ticketless commit on a clean provisioned machine. A regression in the hook (marker renamed, exit code changed, strict default flipped) would ship undetected — the whole point of the ticket discipline (every change starts from a ticket) silently stops being enforced and CI stays green.

## Cost of inaction

The strict ticket gate can regress (wrong exit code, dropped marker, accidental warn-only default) with no test catching it.

## Acceptance criteria

- The deterministic leg vendors/provisions the `require-ticket-before-commit` hook the way a clean rig machine has it, and asserts:
  - no-ticket `git commit` → exit 10 + the `[require-ticket] BLOCKED: no ticket reference` marker on stdout, and
  - a `Closes #1` (or task-created id) commit → exit 0 / allow.
- Runs on every PR (no LLM, no key needed).
- Existing advertised/usable deterministic assertions still pass.

## Notes

Pairs with #16 (harden the real-agent leg). Both land in the same PR.

title: Docker test-cli: guard the vendored require-ticket hook against drift from agent-tools source
body:
## What

`test/docker/require_ticket_before_commit.py` is a VENDORED copy of the canonical hook in agent-tools (`agent-hooks/require-ticket-before-commit/`). Its SYNC header asks for byte-identical sync, but nothing enforces it. If agent-tools changes the stable marker / exit code, `enforce_test.sh` would stay green against a stale copy while a real rig machine behaves differently — exactly what the end-to-end leg is meant to catch.

## Why / impact

The cross-repo contract (`[require-ticket] BLOCKED: no ticket reference` + exit 10) can silently diverge between the vendored fixture and the real hook. The enforcement leg would give false confidence.

## Options

- Record the source file's SHA256 in the SYNC header and add a tiny test asserting the vendored file's SHA matches (catches local edits to the copy, not upstream drift).
- A scheduled CI job that fetches the agent-tools hook and diffs it against the vendored copy (catches upstream drift; needs cross-repo access).
- A `rig`-side check that the consumer's vendored copy matches the catalog version.

## Acceptance criteria

- A mechanical guard (CI or test) fails when the vendored copy diverges from the agent-tools source, OR a documented, scheduled re-sync procedure exists.

Deferred from PR feat/harden-agent-leg-and-enforce-assert (review finding).

title: task --version is a hardcoded 0.1.0 — never bumped, read pyproject dynamically
body:
## Problem

`tasklib/__init__.py` has `__version__ = "0.1.0"` (hardcoded literal), and `tasklib/cli.py` prints it (`--version`, `version=f"task {__version__}"`). Never bumped; pyproject `version` also stuck at `0.1.0`. Same anti-pattern as rig-cli#70 — `--version` is a permanently-stale string.

## Fix

1. Read the declared version dynamically (`importlib.metadata.version(...)` with a `PackageNotFoundError` fallback) instead of the literal.
2. Bump `pyproject.toml` version off `0.1.0` and bump on every release (agent-tools skill `bump-version-on-release`; semver patch/minor/major).
3. Provisioning the agent-tools version-bump ship gate (agent-tools#98 / PR agent-tools#99) then enforces step 2 mechanically.

Follow-up from agent-tools#98.

title: Daemon core: polling due-date reminders (start/stop/status/run + --due + de-dupe)
body:
The minimal shippable **daemon core** slice of the Phase-2 daemon epic — the polling reminder loop, the lifecycle, and the `--due` field. Parent epics: #2 (daemon service + webhooks) and #3 (completion + due-date notifications). This issue is the FIRST concrete increment; webhooks, tmux-inject completion notifications, recurring/escalating reminders, and auto-start-on-call remain in #2/#3.

## What
A `task daemon` subcommand group + a background process that periodically queries the backend for open tickets whose due-date is due-soon or overdue and notifies the CTO.

- `task daemon start` — spawn the background daemon (detached), pid-file, idempotent (never double-start while one is alive).
- `task daemon stop` — stop the running daemon (TERM the pid, clean the pid-file).
- `task daemon status` — running / stale / stopped, with pid + config summary.
- `task daemon run` — the foreground poll loop (what `start` spawns).
- A `--due YYYY-MM-DD` flag on `task new`/`task create` and `task change`, stored backend-portably (a `## Due` body section that round-trips through render/parse for BOTH backends; Linear also gets its native `dueDate` best-effort).
- The loop notifies via the `tg` CLI (`tg --tag report ...`) by default; the notifier command is configurable.
- De-dupe: a state file tracks which (ticket, due-date) pairs were already notified, so a ticket isn't re-notified every tick (re-notifies if the due-date changes or it crosses overdue).
- Config under a `daemon:` block: poll interval, due-soon window (days), the notifier command, enable flag.

## Why
Phase-1 task state is pull-only — nobody is reminded of a due date until they go look. A background watcher that pushes a due/overdue reminder to the CTO's channel is the smallest useful step of the daemon epic and the substrate the later webhook/tmux-inject work builds on.

## User impact
The CTO (and agents) get a due-soon / overdue nudge on their Telegram channel without polling the tracker by hand.

## Cost of inaction
Due dates set on tickets are invisible until someone manually lists and eyeballs them; deadlines silently slip.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `task daemon start` spawns a detached daemon and is idempotent (a second start while alive is a no-op, not a double-spawn).
- [ ] `task daemon stop` stops it and clears the pid-file; `task daemon status` reports running/stale/stopped + pid.
- [ ] `task daemon run` runs the foreground loop: each tick queries open tickets, selects due-soon/overdue ones, notifies, de-dupes.
- [ ] `--due YYYY-MM-DD` round-trips through both backends (set on create, read back on get).
- [ ] The due-date query selects exactly the open + due-soon/overdue tickets (unit-tested against a fake backend).
- [ ] De-dupe: the same (ticket, due-date) is not notified twice; a changed due-date re-notifies.
- [ ] A backend error or a malformed ticket in one tick does not crash the loop (catch + log + continue).
- [ ] A notifier (tg) failure does not wedge the loop.

## Links
- Parent epic: #2
- Parent epic: #3

title: Daemon hardening: PID-identity check on stop + flock singleton (close the TOCTOU + reused-PID gaps)
body:
Deferred from the review of the daemon-core PR (#24). Two known pid-file-daemon limitations the core leaves open; both belong with the shared daemon-supervisor extraction (#2).

## What
1. **PID-identity check before signalling in `stop()`.** `stop` escalates SIGTERM→SIGKILL by the pid in the pid-file with no validation that the pid is still *our* daemon. After a daemon crash the OS can reuse its pid for an unrelated process of the same user; `is_alive` returns true and `stop` would SIGKILL the innocent process. Add a cmdline/identity check (e.g. the process argv contains `tasklib daemon run`) before sending a signal.
2. **flock singleton to close the TOCTOU in `start()`.** `start` checks liveness *before* spawning and the child writes its pid-file only inside `run_loop` after the fork, so two near-simultaneous `start`s both pass the liveness check and both spawn. A flock held by the running daemon (the tg-ctl pattern) makes the singleton race-free and is the real guarantee behind the docstring's "never double-starts".

## Why
The polling core (#24) is correct for single-operator use, but these two gaps make it unsafe under concurrent starts or after a crash+pid-reuse. The fix is the shared `daemon-supervisor` primitive (flock + identity-aware liveness) that #2 plans to extract from tg-ctl — build it there and adopt it here.

## Acceptance
- [ ] `stop()` verifies the target pid is the task daemon (cmdline/identity) before SIGTERM/SIGKILL.
- [ ] A flock held by the live daemon makes `start()` a true singleton (two concurrent starts → one daemon).
- [ ] Shared with tg-ctl via the agent-tools `daemon-supervisor` lib (#2), not duplicated.

## Links
- Parent epic: #2
- Surfaced by the review of: #24

title: task gantt — read-only due-date timeline (Gantt) view
body:
## What
Add a **read-only** `task gantt` command: a terminal Gantt/timeline chart of open tickets
positioned on a date axis by their **due date** (the `--due` field from #26), with a status
marker per row. Box-drawing/ASCII so it renders in any terminal. `--json` emits the same
timeline as a machine-readable structure. Tickets with no due date are shown in a clearly
marked **undated** section (never hidden). The date window auto-fits the tickets' date range
(today is always included). Session/project scoping mirrors `task list`.

This is the **Gantt half** of ROADMAP §1/§2 Phase-2. The closed #1 conflated this with a full
blocks/blocked-by dependency-graph system; this ticket is the smaller, immediately-useful slice
(a due-date timeline visualization), with the dependency-edge graph deferred.

## Why (motivation)
`task list` is a flat list — it gives no at-a-glance sense of *when* things are due or what is
overdue. The daemon (#26) already stores due dates; a timeline view turns that data into a
critical-path picture the agent and the CTO can read in one glance.

## User impact
Anyone using task-cli with due dates: `task gantt` shows the schedule (overdue / due-soon /
later) as a chart instead of scanning a list and doing date math in their head.

## Cost of inaction
Due dates stay invisible until the daemon fires a reminder; no way to see the whole schedule
or spot an overdue cluster. The roadmap's Gantt increment stays unshipped.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `task gantt` renders open tickets as rows on a date axis, a bar per dated ticket, a status marker (todo / in-progress / in-review / overdue / done).
- [ ] Undated tickets are listed in a clearly-marked separate section, never hidden.
- [ ] `--json` emits a deterministic timeline structure (window + per-row bar offsets/spans).
- [ ] Empty case (no tickets) prints a clear message, not a crash; a single-date / degenerate range does not divide-by-zero.
- [ ] The date window auto-fits the tickets' range and always includes today.
- [ ] Session/project scoping mirrors `task list` (`--all`, outside-a-repo grouped view).
- [ ] Layout is computed by a pure function tested deterministically (row/bar positions), not by asserting raw ANSI.

## Screenshots
(none — terminal ASCII view; proof is a deterministic layout test + captured terminal output)

## Links
- Roadmap: agent-tools ROADMAP §1/§2 Phase-2
- Supersedes the Gantt half of #1 (dependency-graph edges deferred)

title: task-cli render: column alignment uses code-point count, not terminal display width (CJK/emoji shear the gantt grid)
body:
## What
Every fixed-width column in task-cli's render paths aligns by `len()` / `str.ljust` / slicing, which count Unicode **code points**, not terminal **cells**. A CJK ideograph (全角) or a wide emoji occupies 2 cells but counts as 1; a combining mark / zero-width joiner occupies 0 cells but counts as 1. So a ticket title with wide or combining characters over- or under-fills its column and shifts every column after it.

Concentrated in the `task gantt` chart: `gantt._truncate` (`len(flat)`, `flat[:width]`), the label gutter `.ljust(LABEL_WIDTH)`, and the undated-label truncation. `list`/`read` are free-flow lines (no padded columns) so the visible grid break is the gantt label gutter + bar area.

## Why (motivation)
A CJK-titled row's bar area starts at the wrong terminal column; the whole chart shears and stops reading as a grid. Flagged during the gantt review (low-priority but real, shared across render paths).

## User impact
Anyone with a non-ASCII (Japanese/Chinese/emoji) ticket title sees a broken, misaligned Gantt chart.

## Cost of inaction
The chart is unreliable for international titles; the misalignment compounds with every wide char in a title.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A shared, stdlib-only display-width helper: `display_width`, cell-aware `pad`, `truncate` (no `wcwidth` dep)
- [ ] `truncate` never splits a wide char or strands a combining mark; adds an ellipsis at the right cell width
- [ ] gantt label gutter + truncation routed through the helper
- [ ] A CJK/emoji-titled gantt row aligns its bar area to the same display column as ASCII rows
- [ ] ASCII-only output is byte-identical to before (no regression)
- [ ] Full suite green, ruff clean

title: daemon: make `status`/`pid_status` identity-aware too (consistency with `stop`'s reused-pid guard)
body:
## What

`tasklib/daemon.py` `stop()` now refuses to signal a recycled pid (verifies the live pid's argv is actually the task daemon via `identify_pid` / the recorded pid-file identity — #25). But `pid_status()` (used by `task daemon status` and `start`'s idempotency check) is still a bare `is_alive(pid)` liveness probe. So after a crash + OS pid-reuse:

- `task daemon stop` correctly says `not-ours` and clears the stale pid-file;
- `task daemon status` still reports the recycled foreign pid as `running`;
- `start` would treat it as `already-running` and not spawn.

The behavior between commands is inconsistent.

## Why deferred

Issue #25 asked for two specific things — a PID-identity check on `stop` + a flock singleton — both shipped. Threading the identity check through `pid_status`/`status`/`start` is a reasonable consistency enhancement but a wider change (every status call would do a `/proc`/`ps` read; `start` idempotency semantics shift), beyond #25's acceptance.

## Acceptance

- `status` reports a recycled-but-foreign pid as `stale`/`not-ours`, not `running`.
- `start` does not treat a recycled foreign pid as `already-running`.
- Reuse the recorded-identity / `identify_pid` machinery already added in #25.

## Provenance

Surfaced by the opus review of the #25 daemon-hardening PR.

title: classifier: resolve model from the shared models.yaml manifest by capability (rig#8 consumer half)
body:
## What

The `task classify` model selection (`tasklib/classify.py`) picks its model from a HARDCODED per-provider fallback chain (`DEFAULT_FALLBACKS`) and the config `classify.fallbacks` list of concrete `(provider, model)` pairs. It does NOT consult the ecosystem's shared model manifest (`agent-tools/lib/contracts/models.yaml`), so the classifier's model pins go stale independently of the manifest the daily cron checker keeps current.

This is the task-cli half of **rig-cli#8** ("Consumers — review board, task-cli classifier — resolve models from the manifest by capability"). The review-cli board is the other half (handled separately).

## Why

Hard-coded model ids drift. rig#8 introduced `models.yaml` + a capability-tagged registry (`agenttools_providers.load_registry` / `resolve_role` / `with_capability`) precisely so consumers resolve by CAPABILITY (`reasoning` / `code` / `fast`) instead of pinning literals. The classifier should be able to ask the manifest for "a fast/cheap model" and get whatever the manifest currently pins, kept fresh by the cron checker — no hand-edit of task-cli.

## User-facing consequence of not fixing

The classifier keeps a second, divergent copy of the model board. When the manifest bumps (a provider deprecates a model), `task classify` silently shells out to a dead model id, the `review just-ask` call fails, and classification quietly biases to the default verdict — a wrong ticket-or-not decision with no visible cause.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A `classify.capability` config key (e.g. `fast` / `reasoning` / `code`) makes the classifier resolve its preferred model from `models.yaml` by that capability/role, via the shared `agenttools_providers` registry.
- [ ] Backward-compatible & additive: with no `classify.capability` set, OR when the manifest / `agenttools_providers` is not importable, behaviour is UNCHANGED (the existing `DEFAULT_FALLBACKS` / `classify.fallbacks` chain still drives selection). task-cli must NOT gain a hard runtime dependency on the manifest being present.
- [ ] The manifest-resolved model is slotted into the existing availability-failover chain (the resolved capability model is preferred when its provider is reachable; the hardcoded chain remains the fallback tail).
- [ ] Unit tests cover: capability resolution from a manifest, graceful fall-through when the manifest/lib is absent, and that the resolved model honours provider availability.

## Provenance

rig-cli#8 acceptance: "Consumers (review board, task-cli classifier) resolve models from the manifest by capability." Shared resolver lives in `agent-tools/lib/agenttools_providers` (`load_registry`, `resolve_role`, `Registry.with_capability`).

title: msgrefs: scope history lookup by bot, not bare message_id
body:
## What
load_history() reads every tg-ctl.<botId>.history.jsonl file into a single dict[int, HistoryRecord] keyed by bare message_id. Telegram message_id is only unique WITHIN one chat/bot, not globally -- on a machine with more than one bot/history file, two files can both contain message_id 42 for entirely different conversations, and the later file in sorted-glob order silently wins. A tg#42 reference would then quote an unrelated (possibly private) message instead of refusing or picking the right one.

> **tg#42** — message not found in local tg-cli history (older than local retention, or tg-cli is not installed here).
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:42 -->

## Why (motivation)
Raised by the automated PR review (chatgpt-codex-connector) on [PR #46](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/pull/46) for the msgref-title + quote-expansion feature ([#45](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/45)): 'Scope history records by bot before quoting.' Deferred out of the original PR as a documented, low-severity limitation (the common case on this machine is exactly one bot/history file) rather than blocking the merge on an architectural change.

## User impact
Someone running task-cli on a machine with MULTIPLE tg-cli bots configured could see a ticket quote text from the wrong conversation, without any indication it happened -- the quote would look legitimate but be entirely unrelated to what tg#<id> was actually referencing.

## Cost of inaction
The single-bot assumption stays silently baked into load_history() with no test or guard for the multi-bot case, so if this machine (or anyone else's) ever adds a second bot, quotes start crossing conversations with no error and no way to tell without manually checking the source history file.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] load_history (or its caller) refuses an ambiguous message_id that appears in more than one bot's history file, rather than silently picking the last one in glob order
- [ ] a test covers two history files sharing the same message_id and asserts the ambiguous case is handled explicitly (refused or disambiguated), not silently merged

title: task-cli should surface stale/stuck tickets on normal usage, without needing pm-cli
body:
## What
task-cli already has a _session_attention_notice mechanism ([tasklib/cli.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/blob/main/tasklib/cli.py#L970)) that warns about stale or recently touched tickets, but ONLY for tickets touched in the CURRENT session (tmux-pane scoped, see [tasklib/session.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/blob/main/tasklib/session.py)'s DEFAULT_DETECT_ORDER), and only as a side effect of running 'task list' / 'task create' / 'task session'. Today's investigation found that the only mechanism that detects general stuck or no-progress tickets (a 24h no-progress SLA, blocker-cleared, duplicate-open, etc.) lives entirely in a separate tool, pm-cli ([pmlib/reminders.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/pm-cli/blob/main/pmlib/reminders.py), [pmlib/intake.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/pm-cli/blob/main/pmlib/intake.py)), which requires its own event store, a 'pm ingest' step, and a cron job to ever surface anything. A user who never touches pm-cli gets ZERO stuck-task awareness from task-cli alone. Proposed fix: extend the existing attention-notice mechanism (or add a new lightweight one) to check ALL of the user's open tickets in the configured backend (Linear or GitHub) -- not just session-scoped ones -- for basic staleness (no update in 24 to 48 hours while in an active or in-progress state), and print a short one-line nudge as a side effect of ANY task invocation. Must be rate-limited (e.g. once per N hours via a local timestamp cache file) so it does not nag on every single command. Sequencing note: this is a proposed feature/design, not urgent. task-cli currently has an OPEN draft PR ([#58](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/pull/58), fixing issue [#57](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/57)) under active review. This issue should NOT be picked up as a PR until [#58](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/pull/58) settles, to avoid concurrent changes to the same repo.

## Why (motivation)
Right now the only code path that detects general stuck or no-progress tickets lives entirely in pm-cli, a separate tool with its own event store, ingest step, and cron job. task-cli's own attention mechanism only looks at the current tmux session's touched tickets, as a side effect of a handful of commands.

## User impact
A user who works only in task-cli (never sets up pm-cli's event store, ingest, and cron pipeline) has no way to learn that an open ticket has gone quiet for days -- it silently rots with no nudge from the tool they actually use day to day.

## Cost of inaction
Stale or stuck tickets keep going unnoticed for every user who does not separately adopt and maintain pm-cli; the awareness gap persists indefinitely and stuck work is only caught by luck or manual review.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A new/extended unit test asserts that a ticket with no backend update in more than 48h while in an active state produces a one-line nudge on a plain 'task list' call with no pm-cli involved.
- [ ] A test asserts the nudge does NOT repeat within the rate-limit window on a second invocation immediately after the first.

title: Global stale-ticket nudge (#59): known scope-limits to close later
body:
## What

Follow-up to #59 (the global stale-ticket nudge on `task list`). During review (`review diff`,
Opus + Codex, 3 rounds) two real gaps were identified and deliberately deferred rather than
folded into #59's PR, because closing them properly means changing the shared
`TicketBackend` protocol / the cross-project aggregation path, not just the new
`tasklib/stale_notice.py` module — a bigger, separate change than a "lightweight nudge."

1. **`task list --all` (and outside a repo) never runs the check.** The nudge is wired only
   into `_list_session_scoped` (the default in-repo `task list` view). `_list_grouped` — the
   cross-project view used by `--all` or when outside any git repo — never calls
   `_global_stale_notice_block`, so a user who mostly runs `task list --all` gets zero
   awareness from this feature.

2. **The rate-limit cache is keyed by a raw display name, not the canonical
   backend-qualified coordinate.** `_global_stale_notice_block` receives `current[0]` (e.g.
   `"owner/repo"` or `"TEAM/project"`), not `Project.coordinate` (`"github-issues:owner/repo"`
   / `"linear:TEAM/project"`). A GitHub repo and a Linear team/project that happen to share the
   same bare name would collide on one cache file and could suppress each other's check for the
   rate-limit window. Low real-world likelihood, but the fix is mechanical once someone's in
   there: pass `Project.coordinate` (or build it) instead of the bare name. Note `_daemon_coordinate`
   (`cmd_daemon`'s per-project state-file keying) has this exact same pattern already — worth
   fixing both together if this is picked up.

## Why (motivation)

Both are real correctness/coverage gaps in the feature #59 shipped, caught by AI code review
before merge. Deferring them was a deliberate scope decision (documented in
`tasklib/stale_notice.py`'s module docstring), not an oversight — but "documented" isn't the
same as "fixed," and both are exactly the kind of thing that's easy to forget once #59 ships.

## User impact

A user who lives in `task list --all` (common outside a single-repo workflow, e.g. someone
tracking several projects) gets no stale-ticket awareness at all from this feature today. The
coordinate-collision case is a much rarer edge case (needs a same-name clash across two
different backends) with a mild consequence (a suppressed nudge for a few hours, never wrong
data).

## Cost of inaction

The `--all` gap silently limits the feature's value for exactly the users who'd benefit most
(people juggling several projects, which is the scenario the underlying task-cli/pm-cli split
was about in the first place). Low urgency, but shouldn't be forgotten indefinitely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `task list --all` (and `task list` run outside any git repo, with `projects:` configured)
      also surfaces the global stale-ticket nudge — either per-project or once aggregated across
      the group, whichever reads cleaner — with a test covering it.
- [ ] The rate-limit cache key uses the canonical backend-qualified coordinate
      (`Project.coordinate`'s format), not the bare display name, with a test asserting a
      same-name GitHub repo and Linear team/project don't share a cache file.

## Links

- #59 (the feature this follows up on)

comments.body:
## Additional deferred findings (review round on PR #71's follow-up commit `b34fc22`, `_scope_to_current_user`)

`review diff --staged` (Claude Opus + Codex, this round) on the reporter-scoping fix found 4 more
real gaps, all deliberately left out of `b34fc22` since fixing them means touching the shared
backend protocol / cross-project rate-limit keying, matching this issue's existing scope-boundary
rationale rather than #59's PR itself.

1. **Reporter filtering happens after the backend's 100-ticket cap.** `_global_stale_notice_block`
   (`tasklib/cli.py:1136`) fetches `backend.list(limit=_LIMIT_INTERACTIVE)` (100) and only then
   filters by reporter. In a shared project where 100+ coworker tickets sort ahead of the user's
   own stale one, the cap excludes it before the filter ever runs — the nudge silently misses a
   real stale ticket. Fix: filter by reporter server-side (query param) or paginate before
   filtering, whichever the backend supports; needs a >100-ticket mixed-reporter regression test.

2. **Reopened GitHub issues stay incorrectly terminal.** `github_issues.py:108` /
   `stale_notice.py:217` — reopening a GitHub issue leaves the task-cli `status:done` /
   `status:cancelled` label in place; `_derive_state` returns a terminal state from the label
   alone while `provider_closed=False` goes unused, so a genuinely-reopened, actively-stale issue
   never surfaces. Needs a tri-state native-state representation where explicit GitHub open/closed
   overrides the label in both directions; test both a reopened "done" and a reopened "cancelled"
   issue.

3. **The new per-user scan still shares a project-only rate-limit cache key.** `cli.py:1134` /
   `stale_notice.py:91` — `should_check`/`mark_checked` are keyed by project coordinate only, not
   project+identity. On a shared machine, user A's check suppresses user B's for the full 4h
   window after a credential switch. Needs identity resolved before rate-limiting, with both
   functions keyed by project+identity; test with two identities on one project.

4. **`current_user` is mandatory in the `TicketBackend` protocol but optional at the call site.**
   `backends/__init__.py:58` / `cli.py:1097` — `_scope_to_current_user` treats a missing
   `current_user` as a normal, fail-open case (matches existing structural backends that predate
   this method), but the protocol itself declares it required, so those backends now fail
   `isinstance(backend, TicketBackend)` / static structural checks. Needs `current_user` modeled
   as a separate optional capability rather than baked into the base protocol; test a backend
   without it against both the protocol check and the CLI's fail-open path.

5. **(P3, minor)** Both `github_issues.py` and `linear.py`'s `current_user()` violate their own
   documented no-raise contract: they catch only `BackendError`, but a malformed 200 response
   raises `JSONDecodeError` directly, which is exactly the "raises" case `_scope_to_current_user`
   was just hardened to tolerate — but it'd be better if the adapters normalized this themselves.
   Catch decode/transport errors inside these best-effort methods too; test a malformed response.

Not folded into `b34fc22` for the same reason #1/#2 above weren't folded into #59: each is a
real fix to shared backend/rate-limit plumbing, not a one-line addition to the new reporter-scope
logic itself.

title: classify auto-create fallback misfires on review-request messages, spawning junk GitHub issues
body:
## What
task classify "<msg>" --create (the tg-cli inbound hook, called on every inbound Telegram message) only distinguishes two verdicts: change (needs a ticket) and justAsk (pure question, no ticket) — see tasklib/classify.py CLASSIFY_PROMPT. There is no third verdict for an actionable command/instruction that should just be EXECUTED (e.g. 'run a read-only code review on the uncommitted diff'), which is neither a pure question nor literally a code/doc/config edit request. The prompt explicitly biases ambiguous cases to 'change' ('most questions to a dev agent are latent change requests'), so review-request-style messages land on change and, with --create, hit _classify_create in tasklib/cli.py (around line 2024), which auto-creates a GitHub issue with placeholder content (why/user_impact/cost_of_inaction = '(needs triage)', a single placeholder acceptance criterion, needs-triage label, and an auto-skip recorded for the acceptance-criteria and user-impact-quality gates). Confirmed 7 times in https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc across 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-12: https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/36 https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/37 https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/48 https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/50 https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/51 https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/54 https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc/issues/55 -- all variations of 'Review the uncommitted git diff / export-format / Workspace-skip diff for cross-file consistency'. Issue #37's body is a byte-for-byte match of the raw fallback template (confirmed via gh issue view), proving the exact code path. The title-similarity dedup in _best_dedup_match (tasklib/cli.py ~2140) also fails to collapse these into one ticket, because each rephrasing produces a low similarity ratio against the prior title, so the same intent (run a review) spawns a fresh issue nearly every time instead of being recognized as a repeat.

## Why (motivation)
The classifier's binary change/justAsk scheme has no category for 'run this existing tool/command directly' requests, and the bias-to-change default silently routes them into ticket auto-creation instead of either invoking the requested action or declining to file anything.

## User impact
Every time someone asks the agent to run a code review, task-cli silently files a junk GitHub issue full of triage placeholders in the client's repo instead of the review actually happening -- the user has to notice the review never ran, manually clean up the spurious issue, and re-ask; across one two-day work session this happened 7 separate times in the same repo, cluttering its issue tracker with near-duplicate placeholder tickets.

## Cost of inaction
The false-positive rate keeps compounding on every review-style inbound message in every client repo using the tg-cli hook, generating more triage debt than real signal and eroding trust in task-cli's auto-created issues.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A review-request-style inbound message (e.g. 'review the uncommitted diff for X') is either routed to actually invoke the review, or is classified in a way that does NOT silently create a placeholder GitHub issue with '(needs triage)' boilerplate
- [ ] The classifier gains a way to distinguish an actionable command/instruction (execute directly, no ticket) from a genuine change request (needs a ticket) and a pure question (no ticket), rather than forcing every message into change-or-justAsk with a bias to change
- [ ] A regression test in the classify/cli test suite covers this classification path using one of the confirmed real-world message texts and asserts it does not produce an auto-created placeholder ticket
- [ ] The title-similarity dedup (_best_dedup_match) is re-evaluated for this failure mode -- either loosened/replaced for repeated review-style requests in the same session, or documented as intentionally out of scope with a reason

title: Fix ambiguous read-time failures and duplicate creation in task new
body:
## What
task new (and _classify_create) could crash with an unhandled exception when the network connection dropped while reading the HTTP response body after GitHub had already returned 201 and created the issue, giving no way to tell success from failure. Separately, task new had no dedup check before creating a ticket, so retrying after any ambiguous result could silently create a duplicate GitHub issue.

## Why (motivation)
Discovered while working on task-cli's own ticket-creation path: a caller retrying task new after a dropped connection during response read could not tell whether the issue was actually created, and could accidentally create a duplicate ticket.

## User impact

title: Session-attention notice can't see a same-team Linear ticket routed through a different project-pinned registry entry
body:
## What's wrong

`task status`/`task change`/etc. run outside a git repo on a Linear ticket id (e.g. `HYP-123`) get routed to whichever registered same-team project's config happens to match first (`_route_id_to_project` in `tasklib/cli.py`). If that routed-to registry entry pins a specific `project:`, the backend's own `session_tickets()`/`list()` filters server-side to that project — so a ticket that actually lives in a DIFFERENT project on the same team is never fetched by that backend at all, even after PR #96's fix correctly attributes its session-sidecar entry to its real project.

Concretely: two registered Linear projects share team `HYP` (`proj-a`, `proj-b`, both with `project:` pinned). A ticket is routed through `proj-a`'s config (first match) but actually lives in `proj-b`. `_record_session_touch` now correctly records the sidecar entry under `linear:HYP/proj-b` (PR #96). But `_print_session_attention_after_mutation`'s subsequent `backend.session_tickets(label)` call — using the SAME proj-a-scoped backend — will never return that ticket, so it can never show up in the "active tasks in this session may need attention" notice, even though its sidecar entry is now correctly attributed.

This is a real, currently-out-of-scope-of-#83 limitation, explicitly documented in `tasklib/cli.py`'s `_session_attention_notice` docstring (search "KNOWN LIMITATION").

## Why this matters

An agent working outside a repo across multiple same-team, project-pinned Linear projects can silently lose track of active tickets it touched earlier in the session, purely because of which project's config happened to win the routing race — even though the underlying data is now correctly recorded.

## User impact

A user/agent juggling several project-pinned Linear projects sharing one team, working outside any git repo, will not get reminded about an active ticket they touched earlier in the session if it happens to live in a different project than whichever config the id-router picked. The reminder just silently doesn't appear — no error, no warning that something was skipped.

## Cost of not fixing

Low-to-medium: only affects users with MULTIPLE project-pinned same-team Linear registry entries working outside a repo — a real but narrower setup than the base cross-repo sidecar leak #83 fixed. The data itself (the sidecar entry) is already correctly recorded post-#96, so nothing is lost permanently — only the interactive reminder is missing for this specific combination.

## Suggested approach

Aggregate `session_tickets()` across every SAME-TEAM registered project (not just the one that happened to route the mutating command), similar to the cross-project aggregation `_list_grouped`/`_known_projects` already do for `task list --all`. Needs its own review-quorum pass given it touches the outside-a-repo query pattern.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `_print_session_attention_after_mutation` (or `_session_attention_notice`) surfaces a session-touched ticket regardless of which same-team project's config was used to route the id that triggered the notice.
- [ ] A real end-to-end test using TWO project-pinned (not team-only) same-team registry entries confirms the notice fires for a ticket in the non-routed project.

Found during review of PR #96 (task-cli#83's 2nd/4th round review, codex + Opus).

title: mark-shipped: a prefixed task code like AGENTTOOLS-412 raises a raw 404 instead of resolving or explaining
body:
## What
The GitHub backend's _issue_number (tasklib/backends/github_issues.py:224-227) only strips a leading '#': it returns the ticket id unchanged otherwise. So backend.get('AGENTTOOLS-412') requests /repos/OWNER/REPO/issues/AGENTTOOLS-412 and the API answers 404. The prefixed forms are not exotic: agent-tools ci/ship/ship.sh derives the code via _review_quorum_extract_ticket, whose accepted pattern is [A-Z][A-Z]+-[0-9]+, and then calls task mark-shipped <code>. The two sides disagree about what a task code is. Note ship.sh itself is NOT at fault and does not hard-fail: it catches the failure and prints a WARNING (ship.sh:2599), and _ship_notify_task_cli returns 0 on every path. The merge succeeds; only the ticket bookkeeping quietly does not happen. A blind numeric-suffix extraction is NOT a safe fix on its own: a code carrying another project's prefix (say SME-ISSUE-185 while shipping in agent-tools) would resolve to agent-tools issue 185 and mark an unrelated ticket shipped. That is the wrong-ticket hazard ship.sh already guards against elsewhere with its digit check. Prefer resolving only when the prefix is known to belong to the current repo, and otherwise failing with a message that names the code and says what to run by hand.

## Why (motivation)
Observed twice in real shipping runs on 2026-08-25: gc-archive PR 229 with code ISSUE-185 and agent-tools PR 416 with code AGENTTOOLS-412 both 404ed at the mark-shipped step. Both merges succeeded, so nothing looked broken, but neither ticket recorded its merge.

## User impact
You ship a pull request, it merges fine, and the ticket it belongs to never shows that it shipped. Nobody notices, because the only sign is one warning line scrolling past in the ship output. Later the ticket still looks unfinished and someone has to reconstruct by hand whether the work actually landed.

## Cost of inaction
Ticket status keeps drifting out of sync with reality on exactly the pull requests that used a descriptive review code, which is the case whenever the reviewed ticket lives in another repo or the code was chosen by hand. That silently defeats the purpose of the mark-shipped hook.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] task mark-shipped with a prefixed code such as AGENTTOOLS-412 either updates the intended ticket or exits with an error naming the code and the repo it was resolved against; it never surfaces a bare HTTP 404
- [ ] A prefixed code whose prefix does not correspond to the current repo is refused rather than silently resolved to a same-numbered issue in the current repo

title: task audit: GitHub-Issues backend can miss a native auto-close (label-first state, no sort=updated), and --revert has no confirmation gate
body:
## What
`task audit`'s Done-ticket scan has three known GitHub-Issues-backend gaps and one general reporting gap, all deferred out of the reconciliation-backstop PR (task audit / cli.cmd_audit) after multi-model review:

1. Ordering/window is unpinned for GitHub. `task audit` fetches `backend.list(state=State.DONE, limit=N)` and treats it as "the most recent Done tickets", but GitHub's REST issues endpoint has no explicit sort param in list() (defaults to created-desc) and there is no pagination — a ticket auto-closed today but created long ago can sit permanently outside the `--limit` window on every run. Fix: pass an explicit `sort=updated&direction=desc` query param to GitHub's list() (mirrors what Linear's list() already does via `orderBy: updatedAt`), or add pagination up to the requested limit.

2. Label-first state derivation makes a native GitHub "Closes #123" auto-close invisible to the audit. `_derive_state` in tasklib/backends/github_issues.py resolves state LABEL-FIRST: `for lbl in labels: if lbl in _LABEL_STATE: return ...`, falling back to native open/closed only when no managed `status:<state>` label is present. When GitHub's own "Closes #123" merge-keyword auto-close flips an issue's native state to closed while leaving its `status:in-review`/`status:todo`/`status:in-progress` label untouched (exactly what happened to https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1347 on Linear, and the GitHub-equivalent scenario `task audit` exists to catch), `list(state=State.DONE)`'s local post-filter discards the ticket because its derived state still reads as the stale label. Two fix directions, both need a design decision:
   a. Give `audit_done_tickets` (tasklib/audit.py) a SEPARATE finding kind keyed on `Ticket.provider_closed` (already exists, already the signal `stale_notice.py` trusts over the derived `state` for exactly this reason) instead of only `ticket.state is State.DONE`. This can likely stay contained to the audit path — it does not require touching `_derive_state`'s priority order itself, only adding a second check.
   b. Alternatively, reconsider `_derive_state`'s priority so a native closed state can override a stale active label — bigger blast radius, affects `task list`, `task find`, and the stale-ticket nudge, not just audit.
   Whichever direction is chosen, add a regression test that pins a natively-closed GitHub row carrying an active managed label, and confirms `task audit` sees it. (Verified while building the audit feature: GitHub's `transition()` → `update()` DOES natively reopen an issue on `--revert`, computing `"state": "open"` for any non-DONE/CANCELLED ticket state — so a revert on this class of ticket, once the audit can see it, will not make the blind spot worse.)

3. `task audit --revert` bulk-mutates every finding (up to `--limit`, currently capped at 100 per run) with no confirmation gate, unlike the repo's existing `--yes` convention documented on `task new`/`task create` ("non-interactive; do not prompt", implying other paths prompt without it). Add a confirmation prompt on a TTY (or require `--yes`) before `--revert` proceeds, consistent with that convention.

4. The report has no "skipped" bucket. When `--revert`'s per-ticket re-check finds a ticket was already fixed since the scan (`tasklib/cli.py`'s `_audit_revert`, the `if not still_bad: continue` branch), that ticket silently disappears from both `reverted` and `revert_errors` while still counting toward the top-level `findings` (and therefore the non-zero exit code) — a `--json` consumer has no way to distinguish "fixed since scan, left alone" from "not attempted for some other reason". Add a `skipped` list to the report/JSON payload for this case.

None of these block the Linear reconciliation fix (HYP-1347) — Linear's `list()` already orders by `updatedAt` and its normalized state is derived directly from the native workflow state (no separate label to diverge), so `task audit` is fully effective against the Linear backend today. These are GitHub-Issues-backend-specific gaps plus one general `--revert` UX gap, found while building and reviewing the audit feature (review-cli, codex + Fable/architect, 4 rounds).

## Why (motivation)
The new 'task audit' reconciliation backstop (added to catch a Done ticket that reached Done outside task-cli, e.g. https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1347) was reviewed across 4 rounds by review-cli (codex + Fable/architect). Several findings apply specifically to the GitHub Issues backend and were deliberately deferred rather than folded into that PR, since fixing them touches shared list()/find()/stale-notice code, not just audit.

## User impact
Anyone using task-cli against a GitHub-Issues-backed repo (the tool's default backend) gets a weaker reconciliation guarantee than a Linear-backed repo: a ticket auto-closed by GitHub's native PR-merge closing keyword, while its managed status label still says active, is currently invisible to 'task audit' -- the exact class of incident the feature exists to catch, just on the other backend. A user relying on 'task audit --json' in a cron job to catch this on GitHub would see a false 'clean' report.

## Cost of inaction
The tool's stated Done-ticket reconciliation guarantee stays silently backend-dependent: solid for Linear, incomplete for GitHub Issues, with no test pinning the gap and no tracked plan to close it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] task audit sees a natively-closed GitHub issue whose managed status label is still active (a regression test pins this: a closed row plus an active status label must appear in a DONE-scoped audit finding)
- [ ] task audit's GitHub fetch is not silently truncated by issue-creation-date ordering -- either an updated-descending sort is added to list()'s query, or pagination covers the requested --limit
- [ ] task audit --revert requires confirmation on a TTY (or --yes) before bulk-mutating findings, consistent with the --yes convention documented on task new/task create
- [ ] the audit report/--json payload distinguishes a ticket skipped because it was already fixed since the scan from one that was not attempted for another reason
- [ ] task audit's behavior outside a git repo (or with multiple projects registered) is deliberate and documented -- either it aggregates across the projects: registry the way list/find already do, or it is explicitly repo-bound and gives the same 3-part WHAT/WHY/HOW error create gives outside a repo, rather than an unhandled resolution error

body:
## What
Add a policy gate so 'task change <id> --what "..."' refuses to overwrite a ticket's What (description) field unless this same working session has run 'task read <id>' (or just created that ticket) within a bounded time window. The read is tracked in a new local marker store, mirroring the existing session sidecar the tool already keeps for scoping 'task list' to the current session, scoped by (backend coordinate, ticket id) pair and a 30-minute TTL. A genuine exception is waived per-command with --skip-read-before-edit "<reason>" (the codebase's existing --skip-<gate> convention), never by a skip persisted from an earlier command. The gate is disable-able per repo via enforce.read_before_edit: false.

title: task change mutates the fetched ticket before policy gates run, so a refused edit can still leak into a later save
body:
## What
cmd_change applies every --field edit (--what, --why, --impact, --title, --due, --label, etc.) directly onto the Ticket object backend.get() returned, and only afterward runs the policy gates (links, user-impact-quality, msgref-title, and now read-before-edit). If a backend's get() can hand back a live, shared object rather than a fresh copy per call (the project's own test double does exactly this, and nothing in the backend protocol forbids a caching real backend from doing the same), a REFUSED edit still leaves that in-memory ticket mutated. Confirmed with the existing links gate (predates this ticket): a --what edit containing a bare code reference is correctly refused (exit code 2), but the ticket's stored 'what' field is already overwritten to the rejected text even though the backend's save/update call was never made. A LATER command that touches an unrelated, gate-exempt field (for example --due) then saves and durably persists the earlier rejected content along with it. Fix: evaluate every edit-time gate BEFORE mutating the fetched ticket object (for example by building the new field values first, or by editing a copy and only assigning it back to the shared object once every gate has passed).

## Why (motivation)
Alex asked for a gate that stops an agent from overwriting a ticket's description without reading it first (task-cli#119). That gate, and every pre-existing edit-time gate, all currently refuse the command's own exit code correctly, but the underlying architecture can still let the rejected content sneak into the backend through an unrelated follow-up command. This defeats the whole point of a refusal-based gate for any backend that shares ticket objects across calls.

## User impact
When someone's edit is rejected because a check found a problem with it, they see an error and reasonably assume nothing changed. But under the hood the rejected content can already be sitting in memory, and a completely unrelated small edit made afterwards (for example just setting a due date) can accidentally save that rejected content too, without anyone asking for it and without a second warning.

## Cost of inaction
A ticket can end up permanently saved with content that a policy check explicitly rejected, with no visible sign to the person who made the follow-up edit that anything unusual happened.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] a reproduction test proves the bug on the existing links gate: create a ticket, run a --what edit that trips the links gate (refused, exit code 2), then run an unrelated exempt metadata edit (for example --due) and assert the ticket's what field was NOT changed to the earlier rejected text
- [ ] after the fix, the same reproduction test passes: a refused edit never appears in a later save, for the links gate, the read-before-edit gate, and at least one other existing edit-time gate

title: task read displays the re-rendered body, not the verbatim backend content, weakening the new read-before-edit gate for legacy tickets
body:
## What
cmd_read (both the JSON and human-output branches) has always printed render(ticket) -- the body RE-DERIVED from the parsed structured fields -- rather than ticket.raw_body, the verbatim content the backend actually returned. For a ticket whose body has hand-authored or otherwise non-canonical sections that do not round-trip through the fixed section template, render(ticket) silently omits that content. This is the SAME underlying gap already tracked for the close-time proof machinery (this repo's own AGENTS.md documents it as a known limitation: task check and task done also regenerate the whole description via render(ticket), dropping manually-authored content that does not round-trip). This ticket is specifically about the NEW consequence for the read-before-edit gate added in task-cli#119: that gate marks a ticket as read as soon as task read finishes printing render(ticket), so a session can be recorded as having read a ticket while never actually seeing content that only exists in raw_body. A subsequent task change --what edit then passes the read-before-edit gate and, on save, silently deletes the unseen content. Fix direction: show the verbatim raw_body (or a diff between raw_body and render(ticket) when they differ) in task read's output before the read is recorded, or otherwise make sure the complete backend content was actually displayed to the session before marking it read.

## Why (motivation)
The read-before-edit gate (task-cli#119) exists specifically so an agent cannot overwrite a ticket's description without having actually seen its current content. A GitHub-native automated code review on the task-cli#119 pull request found that this exact guarantee can be defeated for any ticket carrying legacy or hand-authored content that the structured template does not round-trip, because task read never shows that content in the first place. The gate's core promise only holds if what task read displays is genuinely everything there is to see.

## User impact
Someone could run task read on a ticket, be shown what looks like the whole ticket, then edit and save it -- and part of the original description that was never displayed quietly disappears, with no warning that anything was lost.

## Cost of inaction
The read-before-edit gate gives a false sense of safety for any ticket with legacy or hand-written content: the gate will happily allow an edit that still ends up silently deleting content nobody was shown.

title: links gate: '48px/48px' (CSS size pair) is reported as a bare repo/path reference
body:
## Symptom

`task new … --acceptance "… S1 headline 48px/48px at lg …"` is refused by the `links` gate: `related entities must be links, not bare references: 48px/48px [repo/path]`. Observed 2026-09-06 while filing a ticket for `conloca/landing` (the value is a CSS font-size/line-height pair, not a path).

## Root cause

`tasklib/references.py` `_SLUG_RE = (?<![\w./@-])([A-Za-z0-9][\w.-]*(?:/[A-Za-z0-9][\w.-]*)+)` matches any `token/token` where a segment contains a letter and a "slug signal" (`[.\-_0-9]`). `48px/48px` satisfies both (`48px` has a digit and a letter), so it is reported as a `repo/path`. Verified with `find_unlinked_references`:

```
'S1 headline 48px/48px at lg'  -> [('48px/48px', 'repo/path')]
'body 16/27.2 everywhere'      -> []      (no letters → already excluded)
'file src/foo/bar.ts'          -> [('src/foo/bar.ts', 'repo/path')]   (correct)
```

## Acceptance criteria

1. A slash-joined token whose every segment is a CSS/unit literal — `\d+(\.\d+)?(px|rem|em|%|vh|vw|fr|s|ms)` — is NOT reported (`48px/48px`, `16px/27.2px`, `1.5rem/2rem`, `100vh/100vw`).
2. Real slugs still are: `src/foo/bar.ts`, `owner/repo`, `docs/figma/DESIGN-SPEC.md`.
3. Unit tests for both lists in the references test module.
4. (Optional) the refusal message shows the matched token's `kind` reason so a false positive is diagnosable without reading the regex.

Workaround used: rephrased to "48/48".

## What

Right now tg-ctl treats omp identically to every other non-tmux-detectable harness: features/tg-ctl/unreachable.ts's shapeFor() maps 'omp' to ALWAYS_INTERACTIVE_SHAPE (same bucket as pi/aider/unknown — no headless-mode awareness at all), and the only non-tmux delivery path that exists (tg-cli#306, closed) is a degraded Stop-hook inbox fallback ('delivery deferred until the agent's next turn') built for claude/codex/opencode, not a real synchronous channel. Build a dedicated omp control backend: (1) discover live omp sessions via 'omp ps'/its session DB instead of only tmux pane scanning; (2) deliver a message and get a synchronous reply via '--resume <id> --print --mode=json' (or 'omp acp' if that turns out safer for concurrent access) WITHOUT needing a tmux pane; (3) read the session's own auto-generated title from its session storage instead of deriving a name from the tmux window/cwd. Investigate FIRST whether spawning a concurrent '--resume <id>' process while the original interactive session is still live is safe (the session DB is SQLite in WAL mode — verify it tolerates a concurrent writer, don't assume) before committing to that path; if it is not safe, 'omp acp' or another mechanism may be the right one instead. This is the first concrete case of a broader pattern Alex wants: any harness with its own real control surface should get first-class non-tmux support, not just the degraded universal fallback.

Alex (2026-09-07): 'те харнесы которые могут управляться без tmux должны поддерживаться и без него! Проверь omp например. Ответы на вопросы, отправка сообщений от пользователя агенту и тд. ## Cost of inaction

title: review-cli: role-reuse pool padding never fires when a seat is hard-unavailable (session-limit cooldown), only when merely near its usage limit
body:
## What
select_pool_with_reuse (config.py:781) is the mechanism that lets ONE live model cover MULTIPLE board roles when other role-owning seats are unreachable — built 2026-08-18 specifically per Alex's own request that quorum should be satisfiable by role coverage, not raw model count. It IS wired into the real review diff dispatch path (modes/review.py _mode_review_board, via select_pool_and_reserve_with_reuse) whenever usage_percent is non-None, which cli.py._dispatch passes on every non -m review diff call. But the padding never actually triggers during a real session-limit cooldown event (exactly what has been happening all day: Opus/Sonnet/Fable/GLM in session-limit cooldown, only Codex reachable), because of how the target pool size is computed: n = _effective_pool_size(len(reachable), pool) at config.py:818 clamps n DOWN to len(reachable) whenever pool >= len(reachable) (config.py:711-718, _effective_pool_size). With only 1 reachable seat and a default pool of 3, n becomes 1, so primary = candidates[:1] and extra_needed = n - len(primary) = 0 -- the role-padding loop (lines 834 onward) never runs, because there is nothing left to pad. The padding logic ONLY ever fires for the DIFFERENT case it was actually built for: when reachable has enough DISTINCT models to reach n, but some are near their usage_percent threshold (soft, still-callable-but-expensive) -- under_limit shrinks below n, and the survivors get reused across the missing roles. It was never extended to also cover the harder case (seats fully cooldown-unavailable, excluded from reachable itself), which is the actual failure mode hit today across task-cli#135, agent-tools#597 and others: 0/3 distinct roles from a single live Codex seat, because n collapsed to 1 before padding could even consider it. Confirmed by reading config.py:711-869 and modes/review.py:1258-1336 directly, and cross-checked against ~/.config/review-cli/run-stats.jsonl (every quorum-check-failing run today recorded roles:["consistency"] only, never a padded second/third role, despite Codex being the sole live seat for hours).

## Why (motivation)
Alex, 2026-09-07 (relayed via omp's status report and Alex's own direct question): 'если хоть одна модель есть, значит все должно работать, роли должны автоматом выставляться' (if even one model is available, it should just work, roles should auto-assign) -- this is EXACTLY the reuse mechanism's stated design intent (Alex, 2026-08-18, per select_pool_with_reuse's own docstring/comments), it just has a gap that stops it from firing in the specific failure mode (hard cooldown, not soft usage-limit) that has been blocking review-quorum gates across the whole ecosystem today.

## User impact
Every gh ship review-quorum gate across the ecosystem (task-cli#135, agent-tools#597, rig-cli PRs, etc.) is currently unable to reach 3 distinct roles whenever the Claude-family seats are in session-limit cooldown (a DAILY occurrence per this session's own memory notes on the 5h/7d ceilings), even though the exact mechanism to let one live seat legitimately cover the missing roles already exists in the codebase and was built for precisely this class of problem.

## Cost of inaction
Every future session-limit cooldown event (which recurs multiple times per day per this ecosystem's own history) re-blocks every review-quorum gate ecosystem-wide, forcing either a live Telegram hatch-approval bypass for every single PR or an indefinite wait for the board to recover, even though a single live, healthy reviewer seat is sitting right there able to do the work.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A reachable-but-shrunk board (e.g. 1 of 4 board seats reachable, the rest hard-unavailable/cooldown, not merely near a usage limit) still gets padded to the requested pool_size by reusing the live seat(s) across the remaining board roles, the same way the existing near-usage-limit case already does

- [ ] The existing near-usage-limit reuse behavior (the case this mechanism was originally built for) is unchanged -- no regression in that path's tests
