title: dependency-review CI gate audits the WHOLE dependency tree, blocking every PR regardless of what it actually changes
body:
## What
The shared dependency-review CI slot (ci/dependency-review/dep-audit.sh, provisioned by rig across the ecosystem and product repos alike) runs 'bun audit --audit-level=high' unconditionally on the full lockfile, not scoped to what a given PR's diff actually adds or changes. Live example: hyperide/hyper-saas PR#780 (a pure docs-only AGENTS.md consolidation, zero dependency changes) fails this gate on 6 pre-existing high-severity transitive advisories (browserslist, fast-uri) that were already in the tree before the PR and are completely unrelated to its content. Confirmed via gh api graphql that PR#780 has reviewDecision:null (no GitHub review requirement blocking it at all) -- the dependency-review CI failure is the ONLY real blocker, and it is a false positive relative to what THIS PR actually did. Standard dependency-review tooling (e.g. GitHub's own dependency-review-action) distinguishes 'a vulnerability newly introduced by this PR's diff' from 'a pre-existing vulnerability already on the base branch' and only fails on the former; this script does neither -- it audits base-branch state indiscriminately, so EVERY PR in a repo with any pre-existing high-severity transitive dependency (a near-certainty in any real bun/npm lockfile over time) fails this gate forever, regardless of content, until someone separately bumps the vulnerable package.

## Why (motivation)
Alex, 2026-09-07: relayed omp's incorrect claim that PR#780 needed a GitHub review Approve to unblock -- investigated and found the real blocker is this gate, which is a systemic false-positive pattern that will keep recurring on every future PR in every repo this script is provisioned to, not just hyper-saas#780.

## User impact
Every PR in every repo carrying this shared CI slot is at risk of being permanently blocked by pre-existing, PR-unrelated dependency vulnerabilities -- indistinguishable from a real, PR-caused regression from the CI status alone, wasting investigation time and misleading whoever triages it (as it did here, prompting the wrong 'go get a review approval' diagnosis).

## Cost of inaction
The exact confusion that happened on PR#780 (misdiagnosing a whole-tree audit failure as something else, like a missing review) recurs on every future PR blocked by a pre-existing transitive vulnerability, across every repo using this shared gate, until someone manually chases it down each time.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] dependency-review only fails a PR for a vulnerability that is NEW relative to the PR's base branch (i.e. present in the PR's lockfile but not in the base branch's lockfile), never for a pre-existing one the PR did not introduce
- [ ] A pre-existing high-severity vulnerability already on the base branch is reported as an informational warning (visible, not silently dropped) but does not fail the check or block the PR
- [ ] A regression test reproduces exactly this scenario (a PR with zero dependency changes, a base branch with a pre-existing high-severity transitive vuln) and asserts the check passes
- [ ] hyperide/hyper-saas PR#780 passes dependency-review once the fix is provisioned there (or the fix is verified against an equivalent local reproduction if that repo can't be touched directly)

title: review-threads.yml's pull_request_review/pull_request_review_comment triggers are PR-tamperable, defeating the stale-green protection they claim to add
body:
## What
review-threads.yml added pull_request_review and pull_request_review_comment as new trigger events (a security-hardening change made yesterday, 2026-09-06, sitting uncommitted in several ecosystem repos including rig-cli and tg-cli until this session's resync work surfaced it). GitHub runs a workflow's OWN definition from the PR's merge commit for pull_request_review/pull_request_review_comment events (unlike pull_request_target, which pins the workflow file itself to the base branch and only lets the PR's code run as data) -- so a PR can edit this very YAML file to skip, remove, or replace the review-threads job specifically for review-triggered runs. Concrete bypass path a codex review round found live: a PR gets a green pull_request_target run initially; the PR author then modifies this workflow to skip the job on review events; a reviewer later adds an unresolved inline thread; the review event fires but does not refresh the required status context to red, so the earlier green check stays valid and the PR stays mergeable despite the new unresolved thread. Pinning only the checkout step to a trusted ref protects the review-threads.sh SCRIPT content, but not the PR-controlled workflow YAML that decides whether/how to invoke it at all.

## Why (motivation)
Found by a codex review-cli round today while resyncing this shared CI file across rig-cli's primary checkout (a stale rig-apply-written-but-uncommitted copy from 2026-09-06) -- almost committed verbatim before the review caught it. This is the canonical shared file (owned by agent-tools, propagated to every ecosystem repo via rig apply), so the flaw exists everywhere this workflow is deployed, not just rig-cli.

## User impact
The exact protection this change claims to add (catching a NEW unresolved review thread added after the initial green CI run) can be silently defeated by the PR author itself, on any repo carrying this workflow -- worse than not having the check at all, since it creates a false sense of the gate having been strengthened.

## Cost of inaction
Every repo that receives this workflow via rig apply inherits a security check that looks stronger but is actually bypassable by the exact actor (a PR author) it's meant to catch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The review-triggered recheck path uses a trusted, non-PR-sourced way to decide whether to run/what to run (e.g. a pull_request_target-style indirection, a reusable workflow called from a trusted context, or an equivalent mechanism that cannot source its own execution logic from the PR being reviewed)

## What

title: review-cli dashboard: cache invalidation scans+reparses the WHOLE log corpus (147K files/18GB), never bounded to recent activity
body:
## What
Empirically confirmed live: dashboard /api/runs takes ~3s, /api/stats ~2.6s, the serve process (PID 82914) sustains 77 percent CPU, and 'review dashboard status' falsely reports 'stopped' while the process is demonstrably running and serving traffic (a separate bug worth noting but not this ticket's focus). Root cause traced to reviewlib/dashboard/parser.py's _dir_signature (around line 1286): it unconditionally os.scandir's the ENTIRE log directory (confirmed 147365 files, 18GB on this machine) on every single cache-consistency check, and this scan alone measured 0.58 seconds in isolation. Because signature = (file count, max mtime) and this session has many concurrent review-cli processes actively writing .log files, the max-mtime component moves on nearly every request (confirmed: newest file was 11 seconds old when checked), so load_sessions_cached's single-flight cache (_SingleFlightCache in the same file) almost never stays warm in practice -- it recomputes the 0.58s signature AND triggers a full load_sessions() re-parse over the whole corpus on nearly every request, even though there is ALSO a well-designed persistent per-file SQLite cache (reviewlib/dashboard/call_log_cache.py) that should make individual unchanged-file reads cheap. That per-file cache's own docstring explicitly describes 'a bounded (e.g. 7-day) scan does one indexed SELECT per file it actually needs, never loads entries for the other tens of thousands of files it doesn't care about' as the intended usage pattern (matching review stat --days N) -- but the DASHBOARD's default view (load_sessions_cached with no day-bound) and the _dir_signature check that gates it are NOT bounded this way; both scale with the corpus's total lifetime size, not with recent activity, defeating the very design the per-file cache was built around. Alex had already started an earlier, now-superseded attempt at this exact problem (a stash on branch fix/dashboard-empty-runs-cache, dated well before this session, implementing an earlier single-entry non-single-flight version of this same cache) -- that stash is now obsolete (the current code already has a MORE advanced _SingleFlightCache-based version merged) and should not be reapplied; the actual remaining gap is the unbounded-scan issue described here, which the old stash never addressed either.

## Why (motivation)
Alex, 2026-09-07: 'review-cli dashboard все еще очень медленный, я уже начинал это чинить, найди есть ли уже начало работы и доделай, изучи внимательно в чем дело' -- investigated thoroughly per that request; the old WIP is superseded, this is the real remaining bottleneck.

## User impact
The dashboard is unusably slow (multi-second load, per Alex's own repeated complaints this session) for exactly the users who generate the most review-cli activity -- the more actively someone uses this tool (many parallel review sessions, exactly this machine's own pattern today), the slower their own dashboard becomes, which is backwards: the dashboard's whole purpose is to give a live view of that same activity.

## Cost of inaction
The log directory only grows (147K files today, no retention/rotation found), so the per-request signature-scan cost keeps increasing indefinitely even at today's activity level, and the invalidate-on-every-request behavior recurs every time multiple review-cli processes run concurrently, which is this user's normal working pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

## What
tasklib/daemon.py is a real, working, but scaled-down MVP of the roadmap epic in issues #2

notifications) -- both still OPEN, labeled roadmap. Found unused for two stacked reasons:
(1) task daemon start is never invoked anywhere -- no auto-start on first task call, no
rig-provisioned service/launchd entry; (2) even if started, its CURRENT design only alerts on
one field (due date), and an ecosystem-wide sweep found no ticket sets it, so it polls and
finds nothing forever.

daemon's scope, not a workflow gap to paper over by making due dates mandatory or "encouraged."
A ticket-tracking mechanism should not be gated on an optional field nobody is required to
fill in. Every ticket already carries fields that need no due date at all -- created/updated
timestamps, state, assignee -- so a useful default notifier is staleness/activity-based
("ticket open N days with no update/comment"), with due-date reminders staying an OPT-IN
refinement layered on top for tickets that DO set one, never the only signal the daemon
understands. Widen daemon.py's own scope before deciding whether to wire auto-start.

title: GitHubIssuesBackend.update() reopens a provider-closed issue whose managed label is stale
body:
## What
GitHubIssuesBackend.update() (tasklib/backends/github_issues.py, the update() method) always PATCHes the GitHub issue's native state as "closed" if ticket.state is DONE/CANCELLED, else "open" - it never looks at ticket.provider_closed. When a GitHub issue was closed natively (e.g. a merged PR's Closes reference, or a manual close in the GitHub UI) without task-cli's own status label being updated to match (a drift class stale_notice.py and _derive_state already document), the ticket's derived state still reads as an active state (todo/in-progress/in-review) while provider_closed is True. ANY command that calls backend.update() on such a ticket (task change, task check, task link, task mark-shipped's internal record path, etc.) will PATCH state:open onto GitHub, silently REOPENING an issue the tracker itself considers closed - as a pure side effect of an otherwise-unrelated field edit.

## Why (motivation)
Found during a related review pass on the new task link command: the mirror write can trigger this, and a guard was added scoped to just that one command. But the underlying defect is in the shared backend update path, so task change/task check/any other update() caller can still silently reopen a closed issue whenever the managed label lags the native state. Fixing the general PATCH behavior is out of scope for the ticket that found it (shared code, needs explicit sign-off per house rules) and needs its own investigation into the right general fix.

## User impact
Anyone using task change/task check/other mutating commands on a ticket that was closed outside task-cli (a common real-world case) can unknowingly reopen it on GitHub - it shows back up as an open issue with no visible signal that this happened, confusing anyone tracking the tracker's own issue list.

## Cost of inaction
The mismatch keeps silently reopening tickets across every update-calling command except the one (task link) that now has a narrow guard; issues considered closed keep reappearing as open in GitHub, and nobody can trust a closed-looking ticket to stay closed after any task-cli edit.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Reproduce: a ticket with a stale active managed label but provider_closed=true, edited via task change (not task link), confirms GitHub state PATCHes back to open
- [ ] Decide and implement the general fix (omit state from the PATCH unless intentionally transitioning, or a shared guard/refusal) with a regression test

title: Reject invented task codes; add repo-aware taskref library
body:
## What
task read/status/change currently forwards any string to the tracker. github_issues._issue_number (tasklib/backends/github_issues.py:300) only strips a leading hash and returns the rest unchanged, so invented placeholders (TEST-1, CODE, RIG-CLI-298-VERSION-BUMP, ambiguous-create-dedup) become GitHub issue paths. There is no library that asks 'does this code even look like a ticket for THIS repo's task.yaml/rig.yaml backend?'. Companion attempt: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/612 (agenttools_taskref, not merged); origin https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/607. Alex asks 080/081 from the 175-ask inventory.

## Why (motivation)
A live sweep of review-cli run-stats found thousands of invented, non-resolvable codes recorded as if they were real tickets. Alex: there are no such task codes; validation must consider the repo's own settings (github-issues vs Linear team prefix). Evidence 2026-09-08 on task-cli main 6c8600f: _issue_number('TEST-1') returns 'TEST-1' (same for CODE, HYP-123, free-text slugs) and would be interpolated into GET /repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/TEST-1.

## User impact
When you or an agent types a ticket code this repo cannot have — a Linear-style key in a GitHub-issues repo, a made-up slug, a typo of the team prefix — the tool should refuse immediately and name the real shape (#123 here, TEAM-123 in a Linear repo). Today it pretends the fake code is real, calls the tracker, and you get a cryptic 404. Work then lands against a code that never existed, so later task gate and gh ship cannot find the ticket and the paper trail is garbage.

## Cost of inaction
Agents keep inventing codes (TEST-1, CODE, RIG-CLI-298-VERSION-BUMP). Those strings get written into run-stats, commit messages, and PR bodies. Shipping and acceptance then fail or attach to the wrong ticket, and nobody can tell a typo from a missing issue.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Invented or typo codes (TEST-1, CODE, free-text slugs, a Linear prefix that is not this repo's team) are refused with exit 2 BEFORE any tracker API call, and the error names the repo's expected format.
- [ ] tasklib.taskref.validate(code, repo_root) is the repo-aware library: github-issues accepts only #N or N (or owner/repo#N); linear accepts only the configured team prefix. Real codes still resolve. Proven by tests/test_taskref.py.

title: task change --what truncates text at embedded '## ' markdown headings
body:
## What
task change --what (and task create --what) silently truncates the stored description at the first embedded '## ' markdown heading inside the free-text value. Example: task change TICKET --what $'Intro text.\n\n## Embedded heading\n\nMore text after.' stores only 'Intro text.' -- everything from the embedded heading onward is lost. Root cause: tasklib/render.py's render() serializes each ticket into a single markdown body using '## <Section>' headings; both backends (github_issues.py, linear.py) round-trip every update through render() then parse()/split_sections(), which treats ANY line matching '^##\s+' as a new section boundary -- a function meant to split the ticket's OWN canonical headings, applied indiscriminately to raw user free text embedded in that same body.

## Why (motivation)
Losing arbitrary suffixes of ticket description text -- silently, with no error -- is a correctness bug in the tool every ticket in this project depends on.

## User impact
Anyone writing a --what/--why/--impact/--if-not-done value that happens to contain a markdown heading (a pasted spec excerpt, changelog snippet, or any '## '-prefixed text) gets their ticket silently truncated with no warning.

## Cost of inaction

title: GitHub Issues backend: attach() posts a raw local path instead of a real upload
body:
## What
GitHubIssuesBackend.attach() (tasklib/backends/github_issues.py) currently just posts the LOCAL FILESYSTEM PATH as a plain comment and returns it unchanged -- it never uploads anything. Fix it to upload the file to a permanent, durably-hosted URL (GitHub's own undocumented https://uploads.github.com/user-attachments/assets endpoint, the same one the web UI's own drag-and-drop uses) and register that URL, matching LinearBackend's already-correct native-upload contract. Also fix cli.py's cmd_attach and cmd_change commands, which call backend.attach() and discard its return value, so even a backend that DOES durably upload still embeds the raw local path in the persisted ticket body.

## Why (motivation)
Alex reported (tg#16794) that a screenshot attached via `task check 484 2 --proof history-compare.png` and `task attach 484 history-list.png` on review-cli#484 (the spec-web version-history ticket, GitHub Issues backend) came through as "битый скриншот" ("broken screenshot") in the Telegram task-change notification -- referencing /tmp/specweb-version-demo/history-compare.png and history-list.png. Root cause: GitHubIssuesBackend.attach() has never actually uploaded anything; it posts the raw local path as a comment and calls that "attached". A second, independent bug compounds it for both backends: cli.py's cmd_attach and cmd_change call backend.attach() and throw away its durable-ref return value, so even Linear's already-working native upload wouldn't have fixed the persisted body ref for the `task attach` call path.

> **tg#16794** — Alex, 2026-09-10 05:37 UTC: • implementation: (битый скриншот) screenshot: /tmp/specweb-version-demo/history-compare.png screenshot: /tmp/specweb-ve…
<!-- tasklib:msgref-quote:16794 -->

## User impact
Anyone who isn't the exact machine that captured the screenshot -- a teammate reading the ticket in the GitHub UI, or the Telegram task-change notification Alex actually saw -- gets a permanently broken image link instead of proof of the fix. That is precisely what happened on review-cli#484: Alex called it out directly as "битый скриншот" ("broken screenshot"), which undermines the entire purpose of task-cli's screenshot-proof enforcement (rule 3) if the proof itself can't be viewed by the person it's meant to convince.

## Cost of inaction
Every `task attach`/`task check --proof` on a GitHub Issues-backed ticket keeps silently "attaching" screenshots that are unusable to anyone but the original machine, undermining the screenshot-proof enforcement task-cli exists to guarantee -- and erodes trust in task-cli's own notifications, since a broken image in a Telegram alert reads as a tooling failure, not (as here) a real, identifiable, fixable bug.
